title: Basilica-ble
text:
A minor basilica is not a rank in the Church’s governing hierarchy — it confers no additional jurisdiction — but it is a real and rare honorific, granted directly by the Holy See (via the Congregation for Divine Worship) to a church judged to have particular historical, architectural, or devotional significance, usually in addition to already being a prominent diocesan landmark: a cathedral, a national shrine, or a historically important ethnic parish. The United States has 95 of them, designated between 1907 and 2024, unevenly distributed across dioceses and decades.
The question this analysis asks is narrow and empirical: does the demographic trajectory of the surrounding county — population growth, Catholic institutional depth, urbanization — predict which counties produce a basilica next, and can that pattern be used to rank today’s non-basilica churches on their own “basilica-ble” prospects? This is structurally an event-history problem: a rare, roughly one-per-county-per-generation event, observed against thousands of county-decades that produced no such event. We treat it as a discrete-time hazard model, the standard tool for exactly this data structure.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(tidycensus)
library(pROC)
library(broom)
library(leaflet)
library(reactable)
library(scales)
library(ggiraph)

okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
               "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000")

hav_km <- function(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) {
  R <- 6371
  dlat <- (lat2 - lat1) * pi/180
  dlon <- (lon2 - lon1) * pi/180
  a <- sin(dlat/2)^2 + cos(lat1*pi/180)*cos(lat2*pi/180)*sin(dlon/2)^2
  2*R*asin(pmin(1, sqrt(a)))
}

Source data used, all already present in this project directory:

basilica_designations.csv — the 95 confirmed designations with county FIPS, year, and coordinates.
national_masstimes_scrape.csv — ~23,000 geolocated US Catholic churches, the universe from which the candidate pool is drawn.
arda_ccm_1952_county.xls and arda_longitudinal_1980_2010.xlsx — county-level Catholic adherent and congregation counts, 1952 and 1980/1990/2000/2010 (Roman Catholic Church = GRPCODE == "081").
county_urban_shares_1950/1970/2000/2010.csv — county urban population share snapshots.
NCHSURCodes2013.xlsx — county urban-rural / metro classification (static 2013 vintage, used as a control).
zip_county_crosswalk.csv — ZCTA-to-county crosswalk for assigning candidate churches to counties.
tidycensus::get_decennial() (2010, 2020 county population) and get_acs() (2017-2021 5-year, income/Hispanic/foreign-born share) for the current-period scoring features and descriptive context.

Panel coverage limitation, and how it’s handled: reliable county-level Catholic panel data starts at 1952 (ARDA’s 1952 Churches and Church Membership census) and 1950 (Census urban shares). Eight basilicas were designated before that — 1907, 1926 (x2), 1929, 1937, 1940, 1949, and 1952 itself (which falls exactly on, rather than after, the baseline year and so has no prior trajectory to measure). These 8 are kept in the historical narrative above but excluded from model training, per the project’s stated instructions. The remaining 87 are theoretically usable; two more (Basilica of St. Mary, VA and Basilica of St. Andrew, VA, both independent-city Virginia FIPS codes not covered by the ARDA county panel in the relevant decade) drop out for data-coverage reasons, leaving 85 of 95 basilicas (89%) actually contributing a positive event to model training.

section: III. Method: A Discrete-Time Hazard Panel
text:
III. Method: A Discrete-Time Hazard Panel

IIIa. Risk-set construction
For every county in the NCHS master list, we construct a row for each of five “period-start” snapshots — 1952, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 — carrying that county’s Catholic adherent count, congregation count, total population, and urban-population share as of the snapshot year, plus the change in each since the previous available snapshot. Each row is labeled outcome = 1 if any basilica in that county was designated strictly after the snapshot year and on or before the start of the next snapshot period (i.e., within the subsequent decade-or-so window); outcome = 0 otherwise. A county that has already produced one basilica remains at risk for future periods — real dioceses have produced more than one (Cook County IL and Kings County/Brooklyn NY each have three; five more counties have two), so exclusion-after-first-event would discard real information.


Code
nchs <- read_excel("NCHSURCodes2013.xlsx") %>%
  transmute(
    county_fips = str_pad(as.character(`FIPS code`), 5, pad = "0"),
    cbsa_title  = `CBSA title`,
    ur_type = case_when(
      `2013 code` == 1 ~ "Urban core", `2013 code` == 2 ~ "Suburban",
      `2013 code` %in% 3:4 ~ "Smaller metro", `2013 code` %in% 5:6 ~ "Rural"
    )
  )

ccm_1952 <- read_excel("arda_ccm_1952_county.xls") %>%
  transmute(county_fips = str_pad(as.character(STCODE * 1000 + CCODE), 5, pad = "0"),
            year = 1952, totpop = TOTPOP,
            cath_adh = coalesce(CATH_M, 0), cath_cong = coalesce(CATH_C, 0))

arda_raw <- read_excel("arda_longitudinal_1980_2010.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(county_fips = str_pad(as.character(FIPSMERG), 5, pad = "0"))
cath_arda <- arda_raw %>% filter(GRPCODE == "081") %>%
  transmute(county_fips, year = YEAR, totpop = TOTPOP,
            cath_adh = coalesce(ADHERENT, 0), cath_cong = coalesce(CONGREG, 0))

cath_panel <- bind_rows(ccm_1952, cath_arda) %>%
  distinct(county_fips, year, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(cath_share = cath_adh / totpop)

urb_snaps <- bind_rows(
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_1950.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(snap_year = 1950),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_1970.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(snap_year = 1970),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_2000.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(snap_year = 2000),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_2010.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(snap_year = 2010)
) %>% transmute(county_fips = str_pad(as.character(county_fips), 5, pad = "0"), snap_year, urban_share)

cat(sprintf("Catholic county-year panel: %d rows across %d distinct counties\n",
            nrow(cath_panel), n_distinct(cath_panel$county_fips)))


Catholic county-year panel: 14791 rows across 3111 distinct counties


Code
cat(sprintf("Urban-share snapshots: 1950 n=%d, 1970 n=%d, 2000 n=%d, 2010 n=%d (1950/1970 cover major metro counties only; missing counties are median-imputed by NCHS urban-rural type, flagged)\n",
            sum(urb_snaps$snap_year==1950), sum(urb_snaps$snap_year==1970),
            sum(urb_snaps$snap_year==2000), sum(urb_snaps$snap_year==2010)))


Urban-share snapshots: 1950 n=108, 1970 n=615, 2000 n=3141, 2010 n=3143 (1950/1970 cover major metro counties only; missing counties are median-imputed by NCHS urban-rural type, flagged)




Code
periods <- tribble(
  ~period, ~period_start, ~window_end, ~urban_year_primary, ~urban_year_fallback,
  "1952", 1952, 1980, 1950, NA,
  "1980", 1980, 1990, 1970, 1950,
  "1990", 1990, 2000, 1970, 1950,
  "2000", 2000, 2010, 2000, 1970,
  "2010", 2010, 2024, 2010, 2000
)

cath_wide <- cath_panel %>% select(county_fips, year, totpop, cath_adh, cath_cong, cath_share) %>%
  arrange(county_fips, year)

get_period_features <- function(p_start) {
  cur <- cath_wide %>% filter(year == p_start) %>%
    rename(totpop_now = totpop, cath_adh_now = cath_adh, cath_cong_now = cath_cong, cath_share_now = cath_share)
  prior_year <- cath_wide %>% filter(year < p_start) %>%
    group_by(county_fips) %>% filter(year == max(year)) %>% ungroup() %>%
    rename(totpop_prior = totpop, cath_cong_prior = cath_cong, cath_share_prior = cath_share) %>%
    select(county_fips, totpop_prior, cath_cong_prior, cath_share_prior)
  cur %>% left_join(prior_year, by = "county_fips") %>%
    mutate(has_prior = !is.na(totpop_prior),
           pop_growth = ifelse(has_prior, (totpop_now - totpop_prior)/totpop_prior, 0),
           cath_share_chg = ifelse(has_prior, cath_share_now - cath_share_prior, 0),
           cong_growth = ifelse(has_prior, (cath_cong_now - cath_cong_prior)/(cath_cong_prior+1), 0)) %>%
    select(county_fips, totpop_now, cath_share_now, cath_cong_now, pop_growth, cath_share_chg, cong_growth, has_prior)
}

get_urban <- function(primary_yr, fallback_yr) {
  base <- nchs %>% select(county_fips, ur_type)
  u1 <- urb_snaps %>% filter(snap_year == primary_yr) %>% select(county_fips, urban_share)
  out <- base %>% left_join(u1, by = "county_fips")
  if (!is.na(fallback_yr)) {
    u2 <- urb_snaps %>% filter(snap_year == fallback_yr) %>% select(county_fips, urban_share_fb = urban_share)
    out <- out %>% left_join(u2, by = "county_fips") %>%
      mutate(urban_share = coalesce(urban_share, urban_share_fb)) %>% select(-urban_share_fb)
  }
  out %>% group_by(ur_type) %>%
    mutate(urban_data_missing = is.na(urban_share),
           urban_share = ifelse(is.na(urban_share), median(urban_share, na.rm = TRUE), urban_share)) %>%
    ungroup() %>% mutate(urban_share = coalesce(urban_share, 0.5))
}

panel_list <- list()
for (i in 1:nrow(periods)) {
  p <- periods[i, ]
  feats <- get_period_features(p$period_start)
  urb <- get_urban(p$urban_year_primary, p$urban_year_fallback)
  panel_list[[p$period]] <- feats %>% left_join(urb, by = "county_fips") %>%
    left_join(nchs %>% select(county_fips, cbsa_title), by = "county_fips") %>%
    mutate(period = p$period, period_start = p$period_start, window_end = p$window_end)
}
panel <- bind_rows(panel_list)

panel$outcome <- 0L
for (i in 1:nrow(periods)) {
  p <- periods[i, ]
  event_counties <- unique(basilicas$county_fips[basilicas$year_designated > p$period_start &
                                                   basilicas$year_designated <= p$window_end])
  panel$outcome[panel$period == p$period & panel$county_fips %in% event_counties] <- 1L
}

cat(sprintf("County-period risk set: %d rows, %d positive (basilica-designating) county-periods\n",
            nrow(panel), sum(panel$outcome)))

Before fitting anything, the raw contrast between the 83 positive county-period rows and the ~14,700 negative ones is informative on its own:

  mutate(pop_growth_w = pmin(pmax(pop_growth, -0.5), 2),

The pattern is not “fast-growing frontier of the Church.” Basilica-producing counties are, on average, about 9x more populous and have roughly 7x more Catholic congregations than the typical county-period — but their population and congregation growth rates are slightly below the panel average. Basilica status is conferred on already-large, already-dense Catholic population centers, not on the demographic up-and-comers. This shapes the model specification below and is the central empirical finding of the historical half of this analysis.

title: Basilica-ble
text:
IV. Model: Discrete-Time Hazard Logistic

IVa. Specification
We fit a logistic hazard model with county-level population scale, Catholic institutional depth, growth rates, urbanization, and period fixed effects (to absorb the different overall base rate of designation across eras — the Church slowed the rate of new basilica designations sharply after Vatican II and then accelerated again after 2000):
\[
\Pr(\text{designation}_{i,t}) = \text{logit}^{-1}\big(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(\text{pop}_{i,t}) + \beta_2\, \text{cath\_share}_{i,t} + \beta_3\, \Delta\text{cath\_share}_{i,t} + \beta_4 \log(\text{cath\_cong}_{i,t}) + \beta_5\, \Delta\text{cong}_{i,t} + \beta_6\, \Delta\text{pop}_{i,t} + \beta_7\, \text{urban\_share}_{i,t} + \gamma_t\big)
\]
Given only 85 usable positive events against a risk set of ~14,800 county-periods (a ~0.56% base rate), we follow standard rare-events/case-control practice and fit two versions: Model A, a full logistic regression on the entire risk set, and Model B, a matched case-control design retaining all positives and a stratified 15:1 random sample of controls per period (King & Zeng-style rare-events logistic — under this sampling scheme slope coefficients are approximately unbiased even though the intercept is not, which is exactly what we need since we care about relative ranking, not calibrated absolute probabilities).


Code
panel_m <- panel %>% filter(totpop_now > 0) %>%
  mutate(urban_share = coalesce(urban_share, 0.5),
         log_totpop = log(totpop_now + 1), log_cath_cong = log(cath_cong_now + 1),
         cath_share_now_pct = pmin(cath_share_now * 100, 100),
         cath_share_chg_pct = pmin(pmax(cath_share_chg * 100, -50), 50),
         pop_growth_w = pmin(pmax(pop_growth, -0.5), 2), cong_growth_w = pmin(pmax(cong_growth, -1), 5),
         period = factor(period, levels = c("1952","1980","1990","2000","2010"))) %>%
  filter(is.finite(cath_share_now_pct), is.finite(cath_share_chg_pct), is.finite(log_totpop))

form <- outcome ~ log_totpop + cath_share_now_pct + cath_share_chg_pct +
  log_cath_cong + cong_growth_w + pop_growth_w + urban_share + period

mA <- glm(form, data = panel_m, family = binomial)

set.seed(42)
pos <- panel_m %>% filter(outcome == 1)
neg <- panel_m %>% filter(outcome == 0)
pos_n_by_period <- pos %>% count(period, name = "n_pos")
ctrl <- neg %>% left_join(pos_n_by_period, by = "period") %>% filter(!is.na(n_pos)) %>%
  group_by(period) %>% group_modify(~ slice_sample(.x, n = min(nrow(.x), 15 * .x$n_pos[1]))) %>% ungroup()
cc_data <- bind_rows(pos, ctrl %>% select(-n_pos))
mB <- glm(form, data = cc_data, family = binomial)




Code
coef_tbl <- bind_rows(
  tidy(mA) %>% mutate(model = "Model A: full risk set"),
  tidy(mB) %>% mutate(model = "Model B: 15:1 case-control")

  transmute(model, term, estimate = round(estimate, 3), std.error = round(std.error, 3),

Both specifications agree on direction and rough magnitude for every coefficient. Population scale (log_totpop) and Catholic institutional depth (log_cath_cong) are the strongest, most consistently significant predictors in both models — a doubling of county population raises the log-odds of designation by ~0.67-0.82, and a doubling of Catholic congregation count raises it by ~0.76-1.07. Catholic-share level and change are directionally positive but not statistically significant in either specification — county-wide Catholic concentration matters much less than sheer scale of the existing Catholic institutional footprint.


IVb. Validation

set.seed(123)
k <- 5
panel_m$fold <- NA
panel_m$fold[panel_m$outcome==1] <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out=sum(panel_m$outcome==1)))
panel_m$fold[panel_m$outcome==0] <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out=sum(panel_m$outcome==0)))

for (f in 1:k) {
  m <- glm(form, data = panel_m %>% filter(fold != f), family = binomial)
  te <- panel_m %>% filter(fold == f)
  pred <- predict(m, newdata = te, type = "response")
  cv_preds <- bind_rows(cv_preds, tibble(fold = f, outcome = te$outcome, pred = pred))
}
aucs <- cv_preds %>% group_by(fold) %>% summarize(auc = as.numeric(auc(roc(outcome, pred, quiet = TRUE))))

roc_df <- tibble(fpr = 1 - r_full$specificities, tpr = r_full$sensitivities) %>%
  mutate(tooltip = paste0("FPR: ", round(fpr, 2), ", TPR: ", round(tpr, 2)))

p_roc <- ggplot(roc_df, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr)) +
  geom_line_interactive(aes(tooltip = "Out-of-fold ROC curve"), color = okabe_ito[5], linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point_interactive(aes(tooltip = tooltip, data_id = row_number(fpr)),
                          color = okabe_ito[5], size = 0.6, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Out-of-fold ROC, discrete-time hazard model",
       subtitle = sprintf("Pooled 5-fold CV predictions, AUC = %.3f", mean(aucs$auc)),
       x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()

girafe(ggobj = p_roc, width_svg = 5, height_svg = 5) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_sizing(rescale = TRUE), opts_hover(css = "stroke-width:2;"))






Out-of-fold discrimination is strong for a model built on 85 positive events: mean 5-fold cross-validated AUC = 0.906. Given the small positive count, individual-fold AUCs are somewhat noisy (0.908, 0.883, 0.884, 0.941, 0.911) but consistently well above 0.85. This is a screening/ranking tool, not a calibrated probability forecast — the absolute predicted probabilities below should be read ordinally (who ranks above whom), not as literal likelihoods.

section: V. Candidate Pool: Excluding the 95 Known Basilicas
text:
V. Candidate Pool: Excluding the 95 Known Basilicas
The candidate universe starts from national_masstimes_scrape.csv, restricted to Roman-Latin-rite Parishes, Cathedrals, Missions, and Shrines (Chapels, Colleges/Universities, Military/Airport chaplaincies, Organizations, and Pastoral Centers are dropped as implausible; Eastern Catholic eparchial cathedrals — Ukrainian, Maronite, Syro-Malabar, Byzantine, etc. — are also excluded, since minor basilica designation is, with one documented and out-of-scope exception, a Latin-rite honorific).
Exclusion of the 95 known basilicas is the correctness-critical step here, since church_type_name tagging is unreliable (19 of the 95 are tagged as Cathedral/Shrine/Parish/Mission rather than “Basilica” in the source file). We exclude on two fronts:

Any row already tagged church_type_name == "Basilica" is excluded by construction (dropped from the eligible-type pool entirely).
For every one of the 95 known basilicas, we search the full national_masstimes_scrape.csv for the nearest church by great-circle distance and exclude any candidate-pool row within 100 meters — tight enough to essentially guarantee “same building,” loose enough to catch churches tagged under an entirely different type and a substantially different name than the basilica designation record. This caught, among others, the Philadelphia National Shrine of the Miraculous Medal — tagged in the source file as “The Central Association of the Miraculous Medal” (Shrine), a name with zero string overlap with “Basilica Shrine of Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal,” but geolocated 26 meters away.

nc_raw <- read_csv("national_masstimes_scrape.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_basilica_tagged <- sum(nc_raw$church_type_name == "Basilica", na.rm = TRUE)

nc <- nc_raw %>%
  filter(church_address_country_territory_name == "United States",
         !is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude), is.finite(latitude), is.finite(longitude),
         latitude > 18, latitude < 72, longitude > -180, longitude < -60,
         church_type_name %in% c("Parish", "Cathedral", "Mission", "Shrine"),
         rite_type_name == "Roman-Latin")

excl_flag <- rep(FALSE, nrow(nc))
for (i in 1:nrow(basilicas)) {
  d <- hav_km(nc$latitude, nc$longitude, basilicas$latitude[i], basilicas$longitude[i])
  excl_flag <- excl_flag | (d <= 0.1)
}
match_count <- sum(sapply(1:nrow(basilicas), function(i) {
  d <- hav_km(nc$latitude, nc$longitude, basilicas$latitude[i], basilicas$longitude[i])
  min(d) <= 0.1
}))

candidates <- nc %>% filter(!excl_flag)

cat(sprintf("Eligible-type (Parish/Cathedral/Mission/Shrine, Roman-Latin, US) pool before exclusion: %d\n", nrow(nc)))


Eligible-type (Parish/Cathedral/Mission/Shrine, Roman-Latin, US) pool before exclusion: 17990

Cyril and Methodius in Danville, PA (a different rite than this candidate pool covers), and the Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Honolulu (not present in this particular extract of national_masstimes_scrape.csv at all — nearest match is ~2,900 km away). text:
VI. Scoring: Current County Trajectories
Every county’s most recent decade-over-decade trajectory is assembled the same way the training features were: Catholic congregation count and share as of the last ARDA wave (2010, the panel’s final year), Catholic growth 2000→2010, urban share (2010), and — since ARDA does not extend past 2010 — 2010→2020 decennial Census total population change as the best available recent general-population growth signal. The period fixed effect is set to the “2010” level (nearest observed era; documented assumption that the base hazard rate has not shifted radically since).


Code
pop2010 <- get_decennial(geography = "county", variables = "P001001", year = 2010, sumfile = "sf1") %>%
  transmute(county_fips = GEOID, pop2010 = value)
pop2020 <- get_decennial(geography = "county", variables = "P1_001N", year = 2020) %>%
  transmute(county_fips = GEOID, pop2020 = value)

cath2010 <- cath_panel %>% filter(year == 2010) %>% select(county_fips, cath_cong_2010 = cath_cong, cath_share_2010 = cath_share)
cath2000 <- cath_panel %>% filter(year == 2000) %>% select(county_fips, cath_cong_2000 = cath_cong, cath_share_2000 = cath_share)
urban2010 <- urb_snaps %>% filter(snap_year == 2010) %>% select(county_fips, urban_share_2010 = urban_share)
urban2000 <- urb_snaps %>% filter(snap_year == 2000) %>% select(county_fips, urban_share_2000 = urban_share)

current_panel <- nchs %>% select(county_fips, cbsa_title, ur_type) %>%
  left_join(pop2010, by = "county_fips") %>% left_join(pop2020, by = "county_fips") %>%
  left_join(cath2010, by = "county_fips") %>% left_join(cath2000, by = "county_fips") %>%
  left_join(urban2010, by = "county_fips") %>% left_join(urban2000, by = "county_fips") %>%
  mutate(totpop_now = pop2010, pop_growth = (pop2020 - pop2010) / pop2010,
         cath_share_now = cath_share_2010, cath_share_chg = cath_share_2010 - cath_share_2000,
         cath_cong_now = cath_cong_2010, cong_growth = (cath_cong_2010 - cath_cong_2000)/(cath_cong_2000+1),
         urban_share = coalesce(urban_share_2010, urban_share_2000)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(totpop_now), totpop_now > 0)

current_panel <- current_panel %>% group_by(ur_type) %>%
  mutate(urban_share = ifelse(is.na(urban_share), median(urban_share, na.rm=TRUE), urban_share)) %>%
  ungroup() %>% mutate(urban_share = coalesce(urban_share, 0.5))

current_m <- current_panel %>%
  mutate(log_totpop = log(totpop_now + 1), log_cath_cong = log(cath_cong_now + 1),
         cath_share_now_pct = pmin(cath_share_now * 100, 100),

section: VII. Parish-Level Priors: Church Type, Service Volume, and Founding Era
text:
VII. Parish-Level Priors: Church Type, Service Volume, and Founding Era
The county hazard score alone cannot distinguish between churches within the same county — every parish in Cook County inherits the exact same county_hazard_prob, and (before this section) so did every Shrine within Cook County once the type prior below was applied on top of it. Two more per-building signals, both already present in this project’s source data and both orthogonal to county geography, close that gap: the church’s institutional type (below), its weekly Mass/service volume, and — more thinly — its founding year (Section VIIb).

VIIa. Church-Type Prior
Basilica status is disproportionately conferred on already-prominent churches — cathedrals and shrines — rather than ordinary parishes, and this pattern is visible even in the small, noisy sample of the 22 real basilicas caught by the type-restricted proximity match above:


Code
type_matched <- nc %>% filter(excl_flag) %>% count(church_type_name, name = "n_basilica")
pool_base <- nc %>% count(church_type_name, name = "n_pool")
type_lift <- pool_base %>% left_join(type_matched, by = "church_type_name") %>%
  mutate(n_basilica = coalesce(n_basilica, 0),
         basilica_share = (n_basilica + 1) / (sum(n_basilica) + 4),
         pool_share = n_pool / sum(n_pool), lift = basilica_share / pool_share,
         lift_shrunk = 1 + 0.6 * (lift - 1))

type_lift %>%
  transmute(`Church type` = church_type_name, `Pool size` = comma(n_pool),
            `Among the 22 matched basilicas` = n_basilica,
            `Raw lift (Laplace-smoothed)` = round(lift, 1),
            `Applied (shrunk 60%% toward 1)` = round(lift_shrunk, 2)) %>%

Cathedrals and Shrines are each roughly 20-30x overrepresented among mislabeled-but-real basilicas relative to their tiny share of the overall candidate pool (cathedrals are ~1% of eligible churches but ~1/3 of this small matched sample; shrines are under 1% of the pool but ~1/4 of the sample). Because this comes from only 22 events, we shrink the raw lift 60% of the way back toward 1 (no effect) before applying it, so it nudges rather than dominates the ranking.


VIIb. Parish-Level Signal: Weekly Service Volume and Founding Era
Even with the type prior applied, every Shrine in Cook County still gets an identical score — type is itself a coarse, county-shared bucket, not a per-building feature. Two per-building signals close that remaining gap:

Weekly service/Mass count (n_services), counted directly from national_worship_times.csv (one row per scheduled Mass/service/devotion; summing rows per church gives a direct, near-universally-observed proxy for congregational scale and institutional vitality). Coverage is 17,753 of 17,990 eligible-type churches (99%).
Founding year (founding_year), from founding_years_checkpoint.csv — a text-scraped, regex/LLM-extracted field pulled from parish websites in an earlier pass of this project. Coverage is far thinner (3,336 of 17,990, 19%), so it is treated as a supplementary signal, not a primary one — missingness is handled explicitly below rather than by dropping rows.

Neither source file carries a psuedo_id directly on basilica_designations.csv, so each of the 95 known basilicas is matched to one by great-circle nearest-neighbor, the same approach used for exclusion in Section V but run against the full geocoded church universe (a basilica’s own listing may itself be tagged “Basilica” or something outside Parish/Cathedral/Mission/Shrine, so the stricter Section V candidate pool would systematically miss it) and at a looser 500m threshold (a basilica’s listed coordinates and its national_masstimes_scrape.csv listing can be offset slightly — different building on the same parish campus, rectory vs. church, etc.):


Code
nc_geo <- nc_raw %>%
  filter(church_address_country_territory_name == "United States",
         !is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude), is.finite(latitude), is.finite(longitude),
         latitude > 18, latitude < 72, longitude > -180, longitude < -60)

basilica_psuedo_id <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(basilicas))
for (i in 1:nrow(basilicas)) {
  d <- hav_km(nc_geo$latitude, nc_geo$longitude, basilicas$latitude[i], basilicas$longitude[i])
  j <- which.min(d)
  if (length(j) > 0 && is.finite(d[j]) && d[j] <= 0.5) basilica_psuedo_id[i] <- nc_geo$psuedo_id[j]
}
basilicas_ids <- basilicas %>% mutate(psuedo_id = basilica_psuedo_id)

cat(sprintf("Basilicas matched to a psuedo_id (<=500m): %d / %d\n",
            sum(!is.na(basilica_psuedo_id)), nrow(basilicas)))

93 of 95 match. The two that don’t are the same already-documented out-of-scope cases flagged in Section V: the Trappist abbey at Gethsemani (a monastery, not a parish-directory listing) and the Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Honolulu (not present at all in this extract of national_masstimes_scrape.csv).


Code
worship_times <- read_csv("national_worship_times.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_services_tbl <- worship_times %>% count(psuedo_id, name = "n_services")

founding_years <- read_csv("founding_years_checkpoint.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  select(psuedo_id, founding_year)

pool_ref <- candidates %>% left_join(n_services_tbl, by = "psuedo_id") %>%
  left_join(founding_years, by = "psuedo_id")
pool_med_n_services <- median(pool_ref$n_services, na.rm = TRUE)
pool_med_age <- median(2026 - pool_ref$founding_year, na.rm = TRUE)

# missing n_services/founding_year are imputed to the pool median so a church's score
# is never penalized purely for a data gap; a has_founding_year flag lets the regression
# below absorb any remaining level difference between the known- and unknown-year groups
prep_parish_features <- function(df) {
  df %>% mutate(
    n_services_w = pmin(coalesce(n_services, pool_med_n_services), 40),
    log_n_services = log(n_services_w + 1),
    age = 2026 - founding_year,
    has_founding_year = as.integer(!is.na(age)),
    age_w = coalesce(age, pool_med_age)
  )
}

pool_feat <- prep_parish_features(pool_ref) %>% mutate(outcome = 0L)
basilica_feat <- basilicas_ids %>% filter(!is.na(psuedo_id)) %>%
  left_join(n_services_tbl, by = "psuedo_id") %>% left_join(founding_years, by = "psuedo_id") %>%
  prep_parish_features() %>% mutate(outcome = 1L)

cat(sprintf("Matched basilicas with n_services on file: %d / %d\n",
            sum(!is.na(basilica_feat$n_services)), nrow(basilica_feat)))


Matched basilicas with n_services on file: 92 / 93

cat(sprintf("Matched basilicas with founding_year on file: %d / %d\n",
            sum(basilica_feat$has_founding_year), nrow(basilica_feat)))


Matched basilicas with founding_year on file: 21 / 93

            median(basilica_feat$n_services, na.rm = TRUE), median(pool_feat$n_services, na.rm = TRUE)))


Median weekly services -- basilicas: 12, candidate pool: 8


Code
cat(sprintf("Median founding year (where known) -- basilicas: %.0f, candidate pool: %.0f\n",
            median(basilica_feat$founding_year, na.rm = TRUE), median(pool_feat$founding_year, na.rm = TRUE)))


Median founding year (where known) -- basilicas: 1889, candidate pool: 1922


Basilica weekly service volume runs meaningfully higher than the candidate pool (median 12 vs. 8, roughly 50% more), and basilica founding years, where known, skew about a generation older (median 1889 vs. 1922) — though only 21 of the 93 matched basilicas have a founding year on file, so that second comparison rests on a thin slice.
Given the small positive count (93 matched basilicas, thinner still for the age term) and the correlation likely to exist between “long-established” and “high service volume,” these are fit as two terms of a single small logistic regression rather than as two separately-derived lift tables — this avoids double-counting shared signal and keeps the missingness handling (median-impute plus indicator, as above) principled rather than ad hoc:

  pool_feat %>% select(outcome, log_n_services, age_w, has_founding_year),
  basilica_feat %>% select(outcome, log_n_services, age_w, has_founding_year)
)

Weekly service volume (log_n_services) is a strong, highly significant predictor net of age (p < 0.001) — the clearest single signal in this analysis outside the county-level model itself. Age is positive and significant (older parishes are more basilica-prone, net of service volume), while the missingness flag carries essentially no independent effect, exactly as expected of a term whose only job is to neutralize the imputed value rather than encode real information.
As with the church-type prior, this rests on a small number of positive events, so the fitted probability is converted into a lift relative to the candidate-pool average and shrunk 60% of the way back toward 1 before being applied — the same discipline used in Section VIIa:

candidates_feat <- prep_parish_features(pool_ref)
candidates_feat$parish_prob <- predict(m_parish, newdata = candidates_feat, type = "response")

  mutate(parish_lift_raw = parish_prob / mean(parish_prob),

\[\text{basilica-ble score} = \text{county hazard probability} \times \text{type-prior lift (shrunk)} \times \text{parish-level lift (shrunk)}\]

text:
VIII. The Basilica-ble Ranking


Code
scored <- candidates %>%
  left_join(current_m %>% select(county_fips, cbsa_title, ur_type, totpop_now, pop_growth,
                                  cath_cong_now, cong_growth, cath_share_now, cath_share_chg,
                                  urban_share, county_hazard_prob), by = "county_fips") %>%
  left_join(type_lift %>% select(church_type_name, lift_shrunk), by = "church_type_name") %>%
  left_join(candidates_feat %>% select(psuedo_id, n_services, founding_year, parish_lift_shrunk),
            by = "psuedo_id") %>%
  filter(!is.na(county_hazard_prob)) %>%
  mutate(basilica_ble_score = county_hazard_prob * lift_shrunk * parish_lift_shrunk)

acs_vars <- c(median_income = "B19013_001", hispanic = "B03003_003", total_pop_acs = "B03003_001",
              foreign_born = "B05002_013", total_pop_fb = "B05002_001")

scored <- scored %>% left_join(acs_county, by = "county_fips")

ranked <- scored %>% arrange(desc(basilica_ble_score)) %>% distinct(psuedo_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  transmute(rank = row_number(), church_name = name, diocese = diocese_name,

                     "<br>Rank ", rank, " | Score: ", basilica_ble_score,
                     "<br>Type: ", church_type)
  ) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal_score, values = ~basilica_ble_score, title = "Score", position = "bottomright")

The top-40 table above is necessarily a narrow slice of a 17,666-church pool. To answer a question like “what are the top candidates in the Diocese of Covington” — which will rarely be answerable from a global top 40, since diocese-level ranks are diluted by a handful of very-high-hazard metro counties — the table below covers the entire scored candidate pool, not just the top 50. Type a diocese (or city, or church name) into the search box, or use the column filter boxes; results stay sorted by basilica_ble_score descending, so a diocese’s own top candidates are simply its first few rows once filtered.


Code

  transmute(rank, church_name, diocese, city, state, church_type, county_cbsa,
            n_weekly_services, founding_year, type_prior_lift, parish_prior_lift,
            county_hazard_prob, basilica_ble_score)

    church_name = colDef(name = "Church"),

    city = colDef(name = "City"),

    church_type = colDef(name = "Type"),

Worked examples: searching “Covington” returns only that diocese’s ~14 candidates, all Kenton County, KY parishes with modest county hazard scores (so none crack the global top 40) — St. Anthony (Taylor Mill) tops that filtered list. Searching “Cincinnati” returns the archdiocese’s candidates led by Our Lady of the Holy Spirit Center (Norwood) at global rank 27 and St. Anthony Shrine at rank 76, without having to scroll past unrelated dioceses in between.


Interpretive color
The top of the list is dominated by two recognizable patterns, both consistent with the historical model: archdiocesan cathedrals in large, still-growing Sunbelt metros, and historic ethnic shrine parishes in dense, mature Catholic cities.

Holy Name Cathedral (Chicago) and Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels (Los Angeles) anchor the top of the list because they sit in two of the highest-hazard counties in the country — Cook and Los Angeles are exactly the kind of large, deep, still-growing Catholic population centers the historical model identifies as basilica-producing, and both are already-prominent cathedrals of major US archdioceses.
This is also where the new parish-level layer visibly does its job. In the prior version of this model, every one of Cook County’s ten-plus Shrine-tagged parishes carried an identical county_hazard_prob × type_prior_lift = 9.33 score and landed in a single undifferentiated block at ranks 4-13. With the service-volume/founding-year lift applied, that block spreads out across the ranking on real information: the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe (12 weekly services) now ranks #7 with a parish lift of 1.19, just ahead of St. Stanislaus Kostka (11 services, historic mother church of Chicago Polonia, lift 1.10) at #8, while Jezuicki Ośrodek Milenijny (founded 2001, lift 0.87) falls to #11, the Shrine of Christ the King Sovereign Priest (7 services, lift 0.78) to #21, and the Shrine of Our Lady of Pompeii (6 services, lift 0.70) to #22 — a genuine reordering driven by which of these Cook County shrines is actually running a busy Mass schedule and/or has deep founding-era roots, not just which type tag and county they share.
Sunbelt cathedrals — the Co-Cathedral of the Sacred Heart and Cathedral of Our Lady of Walsingham (Houston), Saints Simon & Jude Cathedral (Phoenix), San Fernando Cathedral (San Antonio, already one of the oldest continuously-used cathedral sanctuaries in the country), Cathedral Shrine of the Virgin of Guadalupe (Dallas), St. James Cathedral (Seattle) — rank in the top 45 on the strength of rapid recent population growth layered on top of already-substantial Catholic institutional depth, precisely the profile that (net of scale) modestly favors designation in the fitted model. Their high, near-universal service volume (many run 15-30+ weekly Masses) keeps the parish-level lift from knocking them back down the way it does a low-service-volume peer in the same county.
Rust Belt cathedrals with deep historical roots but flatter growth — Cathedral of the Most Blessed Sacrament (Detroit), St. Paul Cathedral (Pittsburgh), Cathedral of St. Paul (Worcester), St. John the Evangelist Cathedral (Cleveland) — still rank in the top 70 on population scale and institutional depth alone, echoing the historical finding that scale dominates growth rate; several slide modestly relative to the pre-upgrade ranking once the parish-level lift is applied, since none is an outlier on weekly service volume for its size.

Full output files:

basilica_ble_rankings.csv — top 50 candidates, all score components and descriptive county context.
basilica_ble_rankings_full.csv — the complete scored candidate pool (17666 churches), for anyone who wants to look further down the list or filter to a specific diocese.

title: Basilica-ble
text:
IX. Limitations

Small-N event history. 85 usable positive events is workable for a discrete-time hazard model but leaves individual coefficients (beyond population scale and congregation count) imprecisely estimated; treat the ranking as directional, not as calibrated probability.
County, not parish, resolution for the historical panel. The training data cannot see which church within a basilica-producing county was chosen, only that the county produced one. Section VII layers the church-type prior and the weekly-service/founding-year prior on top of the county score precisely to patch this, and it works — see Section VIII for a concrete before/after example — but both patches are themselves fit on only 93 historical basilica events (21 for the founding-year term specifically) and are not a substitute for a genuinely parish-level historical panel of attendance, architecture, and founding era stretching back to 1952, which does not exist in a consistent form.
The weekly-service and founding-year features are current snapshots, not historical ones. national_worship_times.csv reflects the Mass schedule as currently listed, and founding_years_checkpoint.csv reflects whatever a parish’s website says today — neither captures what the church’s service volume or prominence looked like at the time it might plausibly have been designated. A parish that was a bustling ethnic-immigrant mother church in 1920 but has since shrunk to a handful of weekly Masses will show up here with a low n_services lift despite having exactly the historical profile that has actually produced basilicas; this feature is a present-day prominence proxy layered onto a historical hazard model, not a time-consistent covariate, and should be read that way.
ARDA panel stops at 2010. The “current” scoring period reuses the 2010 period fixed effect and extrapolates Catholic-specific growth from the 2000-2010 ARDA transition; general-population growth is updated through the 2020 Census, but genuinely recent (2010s-2020s) shifts in Catholic adherence specifically are not observable in this data and are a real blind spot, particularly given well-documented post-2010 US Catholic population shifts (Hispanic Catholic growth, Rust Belt Catholic decline) that a full model would want to capture directly rather than via the general ACS Hispanic/foreign-born columns carried here for descriptive context only.
Urban-share coverage gaps in 1950/1970 (108 and 615 counties respectively, vs. ~3,100 total) are handled via median imputation by NCHS urban-rural type with a missingness flag; this is a reasonable but imperfect patch given the source files simply don’t cover most non-metro counties in those years.
Both parish-level priors are estimated from a small number of events — 22 for the type-prior lift, 93 (21 for the age term) for the service-volume/founding-year lift — and both are deliberately shrunk 60% toward no-effect. They are real, historically-grounded patterns, not precise multipliers.
A devotion/patron-saint feature was explored and deliberately not built. Church names in national_masstimes_scrape.csv often encode a devotional or patron-saint identity, and it is tempting to treat that as another parish-level covariate. Inspecting it directly shows why that would be a mistake here: Slavic ethnic-patron parishes (Stanislaus, Adalbert, Josaphat, Casimir, Hyacinth) are real, substantial outliers — 7 of the 95 basilicas (~8.7x their candidate-pool share) — but 100% of that overrepresentation sits in a handful of early-20th-century Northeast/Midwest immigrant cities (Buffalo, Milwaukee, Chicago, Grand Rapids, Chicopee MA, Winona MN, Danville PA). Hispanic/Latin American-coded devotions (Guadalupe and similar Marian titles) show essentially the opposite pattern: only 3 of the 95 basilicas carry one, and all three are colonial-era Spanish mission foundations, not products of the modern (post-1965, and especially post-1990) wave of Hispanic Catholic growth — this despite 220 candidate-pool churches today carrying an explicit Guadalupe/Nuestra Señora-type name. There is essentially no historical basilica precedent tied to the demographic wave that actually dominates contemporary US Catholicism. A devotion-based feature built from the historical designation record would not correct for that lag — it would encode it forward, systematically underweighting exactly the parishes most representative of where the US Catholic population is now. That is a real limitation of any backward-looking model of an institution’s honorific decisions, not something a cleverer feature can paper over, so it is stated here rather than built around.
This is a ranking tool, not a prediction of actual future Vatican decisions, which depend on considerations (architectural merit, devotional history, a bishop’s petition, papal discretion) this analysis cannot observe.

title: Basilica-ble
section: X. Diocese Context: Are Basilicas Outperforming Their Diocese, or Riding Its Trend?
text:
X. Diocese Context: Are Basilicas Outperforming Their Diocese, or Riding Its Trend?
Everything above treats each basilica-producing county as the unit of analysis. It says nothing about whether an individual basilica’s own fortunes are diverging from its diocese’s — a basilica in a shrinking diocese that is itself thriving is a different (and more interesting) story than one that is simply declining in step with everywhere else in the diocese. A newly available long-run panel, reconstructed from digitized editions of The Official Catholic Directory (1888-2021, ocd_historical_panel/ocd_diocese_panel_merged.csv), makes a first pass at that question possible.
What this panel is, and its real limits (read before trusting any single number below): the panel’s total_catholic_population and total_parishes fields are populated two ways — a small set of high-confidence LLM-extracted years (the 14 “decade benchmark” editions, 1890/1900/…/2020, plus 5 gap-filled intermediate years: 1915, 1931, 1945, 1965, 1995) and, for every other edition-year, an older regex/heuristic OCR parse that the panel’s own documentation (ocd_historical_panel/README.md) reports contains outright-implausible values in roughly 8.6% of non-missing rows — single-year OCR “craters” or “spikes” that are not reliably flagged by the source data’s own quality columns. Given that, this section treats the two tiers very differently: the connected trend line below uses only the 19 benchmark/gap-fill years; every other year is plotted as an unconnected grey point for visual context only and never feeds a computed statistic. A lightweight local-outlier filter (comparing each value to the median of its nearest same-diocese neighbors, flagging anything under 40% or over 250% of that local median, applied iteratively) is also run on total_catholic_population before any of this — it visibly cleans up the worst OCR artifacts (e.g. a Detroit 2010/2011 pair that had collapsed to ~1,400 against a true value near 1.4 million) but is not represented as a complete fix, and a few residual anomalies almost certainly remain in the regex-only years still shown in grey.


Code
ocd_panel <- read_csv("ocd_historical_panel/ocd_diocese_panel_merged.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# basilica_designations.csv's diocese_name mostly already matches the OCD panel's
# canonical_diocese_name convention, but needs (a) en-dash -> hyphen normalization
# (the source file was written with typographic en-dashes in joint-see names like
# "Fort Wayne-South Bend") and (b) a handful of manual aliases for cases where the
# panel's canonical name carries a parenthetical state qualifier or full first-name
# form the basilica file doesn't. Built by direct inspection of both files' distinct
# diocese-name lists, not force-matched or guessed.
norm_dash <- function(x) str_replace_all(x, "[‐‑‒–—]", "-")
diocese_alias <- c(
  "San Francisco" = "San Francisco (California)",
  "Saint Louis" = "Saint Louis (Missouri)",
  "Orange" = "Orange in California",
  "Alexandria" = "Alexandria (Louisiana)"
)

basilicas_dm <- basilicas_ids %>%
  mutate(diocese_name_norm = norm_dash(diocese_name),
         canonical_diocese_name = coalesce(diocese_alias[diocese_name_norm], diocese_name_norm))

n_matched <- sum(basilicas_dm$canonical_diocese_name %in% unique(ocd_panel$canonical_diocese_name))
unmatched <- basilicas_dm %>% filter(!canonical_diocese_name %in% unique(ocd_panel$canonical_diocese_name)) %>%
  distinct(basilica_name, diocese_name)

cat(sprintf("Basilica-to-diocese match against the OCD panel: %d / %d\n", n_matched, nrow(basilicas_dm)))

Peter and Paul Basilica in Portland, Maine has no corresponding “Portland (Maine)” entry in the OCD panel at all (only “Portland (Oregon)” is present) — a genuine coverage gap in the source data, not a matching failure.

Xa. Diocese-Level Trend, With Basilica Designation Years Marked
Reliable comparison requires a diocese with real benchmark-year density, not just one or two isolated points. Restricting to dioceses with at least 12 of the 19 possible benchmark/gap-fill years present after cleaning narrows the 93 matched basilicas down to a much smaller, better-supported set:


Code
decade_years <- seq(1890, 2020, 10)
gapfill_years <- c(1915, 1931, 1945, 1965, 1995)
benchmark_years <- c(decade_years, gapfill_years)

# local-neighbor outlier filter for total_catholic_population: compares each
# value against the median of its nearest (up to 3 on each side) same-diocese
# non-missing values, flags anything under 0.4x or over 2.5x that local median,
# and iterates (a single pass can miss a *pair* of adjacent corrupted years that
# happen to agree with each other but disagree with everything around them)
swing_filter_once <- function(v, k = 3) {
  n <- length(v); keep <- rep(TRUE, n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    if (is.na(v[i])) next
    prev_idx <- which(!is.na(v[seq_len(i - 1)])); next_idx <- which(!is.na(v[(i + 1):n]))
    prev_vals <- if (length(prev_idx) > 0) v[tail(prev_idx, k)] else numeric(0)
    next_vals <- if (length(next_idx) > 0) v[i + head(next_idx, k)] else numeric(0)
    nbrs <- c(prev_vals, next_vals)
    if (length(nbrs) >= 2) {
      ratio <- v[i] / median(nbrs)
      if (is.finite(ratio) && (ratio < 0.4 || ratio > 2.5)) keep[i] <- FALSE
    } else if (length(nbrs) == 1) {
      ratio <- v[i] / nbrs
      if (is.finite(ratio) && (ratio < 0.15 || ratio > 6.5)) keep[i] <- FALSE
    }
  }
  v[!keep] <- NA
  v
}
swing_filter <- function(df, val_col) {
  df <- df %>% arrange(year)
  v <- df[[val_col]]
  repeat {
    v2 <- swing_filter_once(v)
    if (sum(is.na(v2)) == sum(is.na(v))) { v <- v2; break }
    v <- v2
  }
  df[[val_col]] <- v
  df
}

diocese_panel <- ocd_panel %>%
  filter(canonical_diocese_name %in% unique(basilicas_dm$canonical_diocese_name)) %>%
  transmute(canonical_diocese_name, year, total_catholic_population, total_parishes) %>%
  mutate(total_catholic_population = ifelse(
    !is.na(total_catholic_population) & total_catholic_population >= 1000 & total_catholic_population <= 6e6,
    total_catholic_population, NA_real_)) %>%
  group_by(canonical_diocese_name) %>%
  group_modify(~ swing_filter(.x, "total_catholic_population")) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(is_benchmark = year %in% benchmark_years)

coverage <- diocese_panel %>% group_by(canonical_diocese_name) %>%
  summarize(n_bench_pop = sum(!is.na(total_catholic_population) & is_benchmark), .groups = "drop")

Xb. Basilica vs. Diocese: A Worked Comparison
The panel above establishes whether a diocese was growing or shrinking around when its basilica was designated and since. It cannot, on its own, say anything about the basilica itself — this project has no historical, church-specific attendance series to compare against. What it does have, reused from Section VII, is each basilica’s current weekly Mass/service count (n_services) and the diocese’s own median weekly service count among its non-basilica Parish/Cathedral/Mission/Shrine listings — a present-day, not historical, read on whether a basilica is running noticeably more or fewer services than the typical parish in its own diocese today. Combining the two gives a defensible (if partial) answer to “is this basilica pulling ahead of, tracking, or falling behind its diocese”:


Code
bench_pop <- diocese_panel %>% filter(is_benchmark, !is.na(total_catholic_population))

nearest_at_or_before <- function(dio, yr) {
  d <- bench_pop %>% filter(canonical_diocese_name == dio, year <= yr)
  if (nrow(d) == 0) return(tibble(year = NA_real_, total_catholic_population = NA_real_))
  d %>% slice_max(year, n = 1) %>% select(year, total_catholic_population)
}
most_recent_bench <- function(dio) {
  d <- bench_pop %>% filter(canonical_diocese_name == dio)
  if (nrow(d) == 0) return(tibble(year = NA_real_, total_catholic_population = NA_real_))
  d %>% slice_max(year, n = 1) %>% select(year, total_catholic_population)
}

diocese_peer_services <- nc %>% filter(diocese_name %in% unique(focus_basilicas$canonical_diocese_name)) %>%
  left_join(n_services_tbl, by = "psuedo_id") %>%
  group_by(diocese_name) %>%
  summarize(peer_median_services = median(n_services, na.rm = TRUE), n_peer_churches = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  rename(canonical_diocese_name = diocese_name)

basilica_context <- focus_basilicas %>%
  left_join(n_services_tbl, by = "psuedo_id") %>%
  left_join(diocese_peer_services, by = "canonical_diocese_name") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    at_desig = list(nearest_at_or_before(canonical_diocese_name, year_designated)),
    at_recent = list(most_recent_bench(canonical_diocese_name)),
    pop_at_desig_year = at_desig$year, pop_at_desig = at_desig$total_catholic_population,
    pop_recent_year = at_recent$year, pop_recent = at_recent$total_catholic_population
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    diocese_pop_pct_change = ifelse(pop_recent_year > pop_at_desig_year,
                                     (pop_recent - pop_at_desig) / pop_at_desig, NA_real_),
    svc_ratio = n_services / peer_median_services,
    standing = case_when(
      is.na(svc_ratio) ~ "no service data",
      svc_ratio >= 1.3 ~ "outperforming",
      svc_ratio <= 0.8 ~ "underperforming",
      TRUE ~ "tracking"
    )
  )

    `Diocese pop., most recent benchmark (2020)` = comma(round(pop_recent)),
    `Diocese pop. chg. since designation` = ifelse(is.na(diocese_pop_pct_change), "too recent to assess",

The “basilica vs. diocese today” column is a current-day cross-section — it says whether a basilica is running more or fewer weekly Masses than a typical parish in its diocese right now, not whether that gap has widened, narrowed, or existed continuously since designation, because no historical basilica-specific service or attendance series exists in this project’s source data to check that against.

Scope note: this comparison was deliberately restricted to the 12 dioceses (18 of 93 matched basilicas) with the deepest benchmark-year coverage in the OCD panel, rather than forced across all 93 — dioceses with only a handful of clean benchmark points (visible in the n_bench_pop coverage table computed above but not shown in the plot) would not support even the modest “growing vs. declining since designation” read attempted here, let alone anything more precise.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
The Roman Catholic Church operates as a series of nested territorial monopolies, assigning every square mile of US soil to a specific parish within a diocese. The territorial assignments were calibrated for a pedestrian-accessible, high-adherence era, and two macroeconomic shifts have eroded that calibration. On the demand side, weekly Mass attendance has declined steadily since the 1960s, generating excess institutional capacity. On the supply side, the urban housing shortage has dramatically increased the opportunity cost of holding surface parking in high-density neighborhoods. The result is a systematic land-economics misallocation: the canonical boundary map no longer tracks where Catholics actually live or worship, and the asset footprint left by underutilized parish buildings and parking generates substantial implied land rents that the institution neither captures nor redeploys.
The economic framework — treating denominations as firms in a religious marketplace (Iannaccone 1998) — captures what the Church is trying to do: allocate ritual services across space. It does not readily explain why the Church consistently resists adapting the territorial map that governs that allocation. The pattern we document across three dioceses is not confusion or inertia. The Löschian benchmark (Lösch 1954) gives us the efficient allocation; the gap between that benchmark and the canonical reality is largest precisely in the metros with the deepest pre-suburban Catholic roots — cities where restructuring would require dismantling the most historically embedded institutional geography.
As one interpretive lens for this institutional conservatism, we draw on René Girard’s analysis of sacrificial substitution (Girard 1972). When the territorial order that constitutes the diocese as an institution is threatened by demographic change, the institution’s characteristic response is to designate individual parishes for closure rather than reorganize the underlying boundary system. We interpret this pattern — which the empirical evidence is consistent with, though cannot decisively establish — as a sacrificial logic: the closing parish serves as a contained offering whose expulsion temporarily restores apparent coherence to a system whose map remains intact. Whether one accepts the Girardian framing or prefers a more conventional institutional-inertia explanation, the empirical pattern is the same: canonical rigidity persists, closures concentrate at predictable nodes in the parish network, and the void left behind is borne spatially by the surrounding community.
The paper proceeds through four movements: theoretical (§II), historical (§III), cross-sectional (§§IV–V), and longitudinal (§§VI–VIII), culminating in a land-economics assessment of the asset residue (§IX).

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
II. Theoretical Framework

IIa. The Löschian Parish: Hotelling, Huff, and the Canonical Leakage Index
We frame the parish as a provider of a public good (ritual services) with a transport-cost sensitive demand function. Following Hotelling (1929), a rational parishioner \(j\) minimizes:
\[C_{ij} = P_i + t \cdot d_{ij}\]
where \(P_i\) is participation cost (tithing/time), \(t\) is transportation cost per unit distance, and \(d_{ij}\) is distance to parish \(i\). In a frictionless market, parish boundaries would form a Voronoi tessellation — each parishioner assigned to their nearest parish. Canonical law instead imposes a boundary \(B\) that may diverge substantially from this natural partition. When \(d_{ij} < d_{ik}\) but parishioner \(j\) is legally assigned to Parish \(k\), spatial leakage exists.
A more realistic formulation treats attendance probability as a continuous gravity function (Huff 1963):
\[P_{ij} = \frac{S_i^\alpha / d_{ij}^\beta}{\sum_k S_k^\alpha / d_{kj}^\beta}\]
where \(S_i\) is parish attractiveness (proxied by weekly service frequency), \(d_{ij}\) is distance, and \(\alpha, \beta\) are estimated elasticity parameters. This generates a continuous leakage surface.
The Canonical Leakage Index (CLI) for parish \(i\) is:
\[\text{CLI}_i = 1 - \frac{\sum_{j \in B_i} P_{ij} \cdot \text{pop}_j}{\sum_{j \in B_i} \text{pop}_j}\]
where \(B_i\) is the set of Census block groups within parish \(i\)’s canonical boundary. A CLI of 0 means perfect retention; a CLI of 1 means complete capture by neighboring parishes. Under the null of no rigidity, \(\mathbb{E}[\text{CLI}]\) should be constant across the urban-rural density gradient. The observed pattern — CLI rising sharply with urban density — is the cross-sectional signature of canonical rigidity.


IIb. The Girardian Diocese: Mimetic Crisis and the Pharmakos
Girard (1972) argues that social order is constituted through differentiation — the drawing of distinctions that prevent the undifferentiated mimetic rivalry he calls the “crisis of differences.” Sacred boundaries are the primary instrument of that differentiation. In the Catholic diocesan context, canonical territorial boundaries are not merely administrative lines: they are the spatial expression of a differentiating order that assigns every Catholic body to a specific sacred jurisdiction, distinguishing each parish from its neighbors through the particularity of territory, history, and community.
This differentiating order was stable so long as the parish’s canonical boundary and its social community were roughly coextensive — which they were in the pedestrian city of the early 20th century. The parish was the neighborhood; the neighborhood was the parish; the boundary between them was both canonical and social. Postwar automobile mobility dissolved this coextension without dissolving the canonical map. Populations migrated outward; boundaries did not. The canonical distinctions that maintained order now float free of the social reality they were meant to organize. This is what Girard would recognize as mimetic undifferentiation: the boundaries are still drawn, but the differences they mark have ceased to correspond to anything outside themselves.
The institution’s characteristic response to a crisis of differences is the scapegoat mechanism (Girard 1986). Rather than reorganize the differentiating order — which would require acknowledging that the order itself is contingent — the institution designates a pharmakos whose expulsion restores apparent coherence. The scapegoat is selected not because it is the cause of the crisis, but because it is sufficiently marginal and sufficiently distinguishable to serve as its symbolic container. In the diocesan restructuring process, the pharmakos is the parish marked for closure. It is selected on attendance and financial metrics — measures of its own weakness — while the canonical map that produced its weakness is left untouched. Each closure is announced as a rational response to demographic reality. What it actually accomplishes is the preservation of the territorial fiction by consuming one of its weakest nodes.
The empirical implication is testable: if the diocese operates sacrificial logic, then high-CLI parishes — those whose canonical boundaries have become most fictive, most divorced from their actual social catchment — should face elevated closure risk, controlling for their absolute scale of decline. The misallocation itself should predict the sacrifice.

section: III. Historical Origins: The Making of the Misallocation
text:
III. Historical Origins: The Making of the Misallocation
The CLI framework measures the current state of canonical rigidity but does not explain why the misallocation is deepest in the metros where it is most entrenched. That explanation requires a historical lens. Suburbanization is the triggering event of the mimetic crisis: the moment when the pedestrian map of the early 20th century stopped matching the automobile geography that replaced it. The congregation-trend data show that high-CLI metros are precisely those with the deepest pre-suburban Catholic institutional roots — cities where the parish network was so dense before the postwar wave that the institution never fully relocated outward with its membership. The Q5 metros (Boston, Chicago, Detroit, Milwaukee, Providence) had the most differentiated pre-suburban parish geography to lose, which is why the mimetic crisis is deepest there.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
IV. Data

Parish locations and service frequencies: ~23,000 geolocated US Catholic institutions scraped from national directories, with weekend and weekday Mass counts as the primary service-intensity proxy.
Infrastructure footprints: Overture Maps (May 2026 release), queried via DuckDB, providing AI-derived parking area estimates in square meters per site.
Demographics: ACS 5-Year Estimates at the Census tract level for population density, population change (2000–2020), and housing vacancy.
ARDA Longitudinal Congregations and Membership Study (1980–2010): County-level Catholic congregation and adherent counts at four decennial time points, joined to NCHS 2013 urban-rural classification codes.
1952 Churches and Church Membership (National Council of Churches): County-level Catholic congregation and membership counts providing the pre-suburbanization baseline.
Archdiocese of Detroit Parish Restructuring Workbooks (2025-26): For each of 209 active AOD parishes: sacramental trend data (2015–2024), deferred maintenance estimates, founding year histories, and territorial cohesion statistics (share of registered parishioners residing within canonical boundary).
Archdiocese of Cincinnati Sacramental Panel (1999-2025): 234 parishes, 20 statistics, 26 years. Founding years recovered for 118/120 Cincinnati-area parishes via targeted LLM extraction using Gemini 2.5 Flash. Mass attendance panel (2015–2025, church-level, with seating capacity and utilization).
Two-diocese pooled dataset: 240 parishes (121 Detroit, 119 Cincinnati) with founding lags, sacramental % changes 2015–2024, and cohort assignments.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
section: V. The CLI in Cross-Section: Where the Map Has Failed
text:
V. The CLI in Cross-Section: Where the Map Has Failed

Va. The Ohio River: A Boundary That Cannot Be Dissolved
The Ohio River marks a state boundary and a diocesan boundary simultaneously. The Archdiocese of Cincinnati and the Diocese of Covington are legally distinct markets. But the urban fabric is continuous: downtown Cincinnati parishes are geographically closer to many Northern Kentucky residents than their own diocesan alternatives. Voronoi analysis shows that over 30% of the Cincinnati CBD’s natural catchment technically sits in the Diocese of Covington.


Code
church_data_map <- read_csv("national_masstimes_scrape.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(church_address_country_territory_name == "United States", !is.na(latitude))

cin_cov <- church_data_map %>%
  filter(diocese_name %in% c("Cincinnati", "Covington")) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(32616)

voronoi_cin_cov <- st_voronoi(st_union(cin_cov)) %>%
  st_collection_extract() %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  st_join(cin_cov) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

pal <- colorFactor(palette = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), domain = cin_cov$diocese_name)

leaflet(voronoi_cin_cov) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(diocese_name), fillOpacity = 0.4, color = "white", weight = 1,
              popup = ~paste("<b>", name, "</b><br>Diocese:", diocese_name)) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~diocese_name, title = "Diocese Natural Market Area")






The Ohio River case is the most legible instantiation of canonical rigidity because the physical boundary coincides exactly with the diocesan boundary. The river did not move; it is the parish infrastructure — frozen in place by canonical law — that has failed to adapt to the bridges, commuting patterns, and residential dispersal that now connect Cincinnati and Covington as a single metropolitan labor and worship market. Unlike a purely administrative boundary, the Ohio River boundary cannot be dissolved through restructuring: canonical leakage is made permanently visible here because the institutional response that manages it elsewhere — closure and merger — is not available across a diocesan line defined by state and territory.


Vb. New York / Brooklyn and Chicago / Joliet
These cases validate the pattern along political rather than physical boundaries: state lines that are simultaneously diocesan boundaries produce the same leakage signature as the river, but with greater administrative ambiguity about which institution bears responsibility for the misallocation.


Vc. Street-Level Evidence: Pedestrian Infrastructure Near Parishes
If closure selection concentrates on marginal parishes, one plausible spatial correlate is pedestrian infrastructure: parishes surrounded by fewer walkable streets and destinations (POIs) would be more peripheral and potentially more vulnerable to institutional selection. We test this by computing a composite pedestrian score for each parish in all three dioceses — a 500m-buffer-weighted sum of safe-walking infrastructure (footways, paths, pedestrian streets scored 5; residential streets scored 3; others scored 1) combined with POI density — and then comparing scores between parishes classified as open versus at-risk or low-attendance.

Philadelphia’s surviving-parish comparison reinforces the same pattern. Parishes in the bottom attendance quartile (the weakest survivors of Project HOME’s 2012–13 restructuring wave) have a mean composite pedestrian score of 25.1, significantly higher than the upper three quartiles (11.4; t = -4.98, p < 0.001).
The pedestrian infrastructure gap between at-risk and surviving parishes runs consistently in the positive direction: weaker parishes are located in more walkable surroundings. This is the inverse of the initial hypothesis but is consistent with the founding cohort story. Pre-suburban parishes — the oldest, least-declining in absolute scale, but most exposed to population out-migration — are concentrated in dense urban cores where pedestrian infrastructure is highest. The suburban and exurban parishes that have retained relative attendance vitality are in lower-density areas with fewer footways and POIs within 500 meters. Pedestrian infrastructure tracks urban density, which tracks founding era, which tracks the leapfrog misallocation. The street-level evidence does not support a simple peripheral-selection narrative; it suggests instead that the parishes most at risk are, paradoxically, the most centrally and walkably located — stranded in neighborhoods that were built for them and have since moved on.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
section: VI. Detroit: Closures, Spatial Voids, and Clustering
text:
VI. Detroit: Closures, Spatial Voids, and Clustering
Detroit is the diocese where the arc of canonical misallocation has advanced furthest: a deeply pre-suburban institutional footprint, accelerated population loss from the opioid era and deindustrialization, and a formal restructuring process (the AOD’s 2025-26 “Act of Accompaniment”) that makes the closure-selection mechanism observable in near-real time. The data let us examine the structural pattern — cohort gradients, territorial cohesion, spatial clustering — and the institutional response to it.


Code
library(fuzzyjoin)
library(stringdist)

aod <- read_csv("aod_parish_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
geo <- read_csv("aod_geography.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(path, pct_within_parish, pct_outside_region)
aod <- aod |> left_join(geo, by = "path")

zip_county_aod <- read_csv("zip_county_crosswalk.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(
    zip         = str_pad(as.character(ZCTA5), 5, pad = "0"),
    county_fips = str_pad(as.character(GEOID), 5, pad = "0")
  ) |>
  group_by(zip) |> slice(1) |> ungroup()

fy <- read_csv("founding_years_checkpoint.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(psuedo_id, founding_year_llm = founding_year)

mt_mi <- read_csv("national_masstimes_scrape.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(
    church_address_country_territory_name == "United States",
    str_detect(church_address_county, "Wayne|Oakland|Macomb|Monroe|Washtenaw|Livingston")
  ) |>
  select(psuedo_id, name, church_address_postal_code) |>
  left_join(fy, by = "psuedo_id") |>
  mutate(zip = str_pad(str_sub(church_address_postal_code, 1, 5), 5, pad = "0")) |>
  left_join(zip_county_aod, by = "zip")

urb_snaps <- bind_rows(
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_1950.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 1950),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_1970.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 1970),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_2000.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 2000),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_2010.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 2010)
)
crossing_yr <- urb_snaps |>
  arrange(county_fips, snap_year) |>
  group_by(county_fips) |>
  group_modify(function(d, k) {
    d <- arrange(d, snap_year)
    crossed <- d$suburban_share >= 0.40
    if (!any(crossed)) return(tibble(cross_year = NA_real_))
    fi <- which(crossed)[1]
    if (fi == 1) return(tibble(cross_year = d$snap_year[1] - 10))
    y0 <- d$snap_year[fi-1]; s0 <- d$suburban_share[fi-1]
    y1 <- d$snap_year[fi];   s1 <- d$suburban_share[fi]
    tibble(cross_year = y0 + (0.40 - s0) / (s1 - s0) * (y1 - y0))
  }) |>
  ungroup()

mt_mi <- mt_mi |> left_join(crossing_yr, by = "county_fips")

clean_nm <- function(x) {
  x |> str_to_lower() |>
    str_remove("\\s+parish$|\\s+church$") |>
    str_remove_all("[^a-z ]") |> str_squish()
}

mt2  <- mt_mi |> mutate(name_key = clean_nm(name))

  group_by(path) |>

  ungroup()

  mutate(

      founding_lag <  20   ~ "Early post-suburban\n(1950s–60s)",
      founding_lag <  40   ~ "Late post-suburban\n(1970s–80s)",

Post-suburban parishes founded in the 1950s and 60s — built to serve the first generation of Catholic suburbanites — show the sharpest sacramental decline: baptisms fell –40.8% and confirmations –40.7%, compared with –23.7% and –23.0% for pre-suburban parishes. The exurban cohort is worst of all at –48% baptisms.
One interpretation: pre-suburban parishes retain a residual differentiated identity — the Polish parish, the Italian parish, the heritage basilica — that provides a social anchor even as surrounding populations change. Post-suburban parishes were built for a generic Catholic suburbanite with no ethnic or historical marker, making them more easily substituted by no-church-at-all as attendance declines. The founding lag is not the cause of decline but a proxy for the degree to which a parish’s identity is anchored in a specific community versus a generic spatial assignment. Whether one frames this through Girard’s vocabulary of differentiation or through a simpler institutional-sociology account of community embeddedness, the gradient is empirically robust.

text:
VIIc. Philadelphia: A Third Diocese Under Financial Stress
Philadelphia is the oldest Catholic diocese in the United States (established 1808), with parishes dating to 1733 — a colonial-era depth absent from Detroit and Cincinnati. Its crisis trigger differs from the AOD collapse: the Archdiocese of Philadelphia faced cascading financial pressure from clergy abuse settlements culminating in the 2011 grand jury report, prompting the Project HOME restructuring that began closing and merging parishes in 2012. The structural features of the restructuring are comparable — a crisis, a deliberative process, a selection of parishes for closure — but the driving mechanism is financial shock rather than population collapse. Philadelphia thus provides a cross-crisis generalizability check: does the same spatial pattern of misallocation appear when the trigger is financial rather than demographic?

The baseline decline of –46.6 attendees/year (p < 0.001) is steeper in absolute terms than Cincinnati’s pre-crisis trajectory and consistent with a diocese already mid-shock during the 2012-2021 window. The founding lag × time interaction is β = –0.151 (p < 0.001) — the opposite sign from the null interaction in Detroit and Cincinnati. This sign flip should be read carefully: in Detroit and Cincinnati, founding era predicts the level of sacramental vitality but not the rate of decline. In Philadelphia, parishes with greater founding lag (newer, post-suburban) are declining faster. The most likely explanation is the thin post-suburban tail: with only 8 parishes founded after 1960, the late-founding cohort is poorly identified and subject to high leverage from a handful of outer-ring parishes that were disproportionately targeted in Project HOME’s first wave of closures. The interaction captures the restructuring shock differentially hitting the periphery, not a reversal of the structural pattern documented in Detroit and Cincinnati.


VIIc-iv. Selection Pattern
Project HOME designated 49 parishes for closure or merger beginning in 2012. The selection criteria — attendance levels, financial viability, building condition — are consistent with those applied in the Detroit AOD restructuring, and the spatial pattern is similar: Philadelphia’s pre-industrial parishes (Old St. Joseph’s, Old St. Mary’s, St. Augustine’s) were spared; closure concentrated on the outer ring despite that ring holding the smallest share of total parish population. We interpret this as consistent with, though not proof of, a selection logic that targets institutionally weakest nodes while preserving the canonical map that produced their weakness. The mechanism here is financial rather than demographic, but the structural result — canonical rigidity maintained through closure of peripheral nodes — is the same.

The signal is consistent in sign with both single-diocese estimates but is attenuated across dioceses because the AOD crisis amplifier — whatever additional mechanism drives Detroit’s severity — is diocese-specific and absorbed by the FE. The structural pattern (lag → level) generalizes; the severity of the crisis does not.
Philadelphia enters as a third data point but with important caveats for pooled inference: the panel covers 2012-2021 (10 years vs. 26 for Cincinnati) and lacks confirmations data, so it enters any pooled specification with a diocese fixed effect but cannot contribute to the sacramental diversity outcomes used in the two-diocese models. The sign reversal on the founding lag × time interaction (β = –0.151 in Philadelphia vs. near-zero nulls in Detroit and Cincinnati) signals genuine cross-diocese heterogeneity in the rate dynamics — likely driven by the thin post-suburban tail and the contemporaneous restructuring shock — and reinforces that the founding lag’s primary signal is in levels, not trends. Future pooled analysis adding Philadelphia should use attendance as the common outcome and allow the lag-trend interaction to vary by diocese.
The two-diocese setup supports a natural extrapolation: applying the Cincinnati β (no crisis amplifier) to the national founding lag distribution in national_lag_analysis.csv (939 parishes, 73 CBSAs) gives a lower-bound estimate of structural sacramental capacity loss. Detroit’s β gives the upper bound. The gap between them is the quantitative footprint of a diocesan crisis — the difference between structural rigidity and structural rigidity plus institutional collapse.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
X. Conclusion
The canonical boundary map that governs American Catholic parishes was calibrated for a pedestrian, high-adherence 19th century. The data across three dioceses — 23,000 national parishes, 175 AOD restructuring workbooks, and 26 years of sacramental panels — show consistently that the map has not adapted to the automobile geography and secular decline of the postwar era. The Canonical Leakage Index rises with urban density and pre-suburban Catholic depth, peaking in precisely the metros (Boston, Chicago, Detroit, Milwaukee, Providence) where diocesan boundaries are most historically entrenched.
What we can say with confidence: founding era predicts the level of sacramental activity in a parish — pre-suburban parishes are healthier, post-suburban and exurban parishes are the most distressed — but does not predict the rate of decline. This null interaction holds in Detroit (a diocese in formal crisis) and Cincinnati (a diocese earlier in the same trajectory), across two independent identification strategies. It is robust to diocese fixed effects in a pooled specification, though the AOD severity amplifier is diocese-specific.
What we can say with somewhat less confidence: the closure selection process, when it arrives, concentrates on institutionally weaker nodes while leaving the canonical boundary map intact. This is documented most directly in Philadelphia (Project HOME) and is consistent with what can be inferred from the AOD Act 2 restructuring workbooks. Whether this pattern reflects a Girardian sacrificial logic — an institutional mechanism that preserves the differentiating order by consuming its weakest nodes — or a more mundane process of financial triage and episcopal politics, the empirical pattern is the same. We invoke the Girardian frame not as a claim about the intentions of diocesan administrators but as an interpretive lens for why the map, rather than the individual parish, is consistently the preserved element.
What the street-level pedestrian infrastructure evidence adds: the parishes most at risk in both Detroit and Philadelphia are not the geographically peripheral ones with poor walkable surroundings. They are, if anything, more walkably located — concentrated in dense urban cores where pedestrian infrastructure is richest but where the Catholic population most thoroughly out-migrated in the postwar decades. The spatial selection mechanism is not peripheral-to-center but rather a stranding: parishes built into walkable urban neighborhoods that no longer hold their founding populations.
The structural finding has a precise policy implication. The institution cannot close the misallocation gap by making individual parishes more vital — the level effect is set by founding era, and pastoral renewal does not change the founding year. Reorganization requires either external shock sufficient to force territorial restructuring (as in Detroit) or a theological reframing that decouples canonical territory from sacred identity — making the map a convenience rather than a constitution. The asset-side residue of the current equilibrium — underutilized urban land held in institutional limbo — represents a quantifiable cost of that rigidity, borne by the housing markets and communities that surround the void.

title: Canonical Rigidity & Sacred Space
text:
The Roman Catholic Church in the United States operates an inherited spatial infrastructure — approximately 23,000 geolocated parishes — whose boundaries were drawn for a pedestrian-accessible, high-adherence 19th century. This project examines what happens when those legacy structures meet 21st-century demographic realities: automobile mobility, declining participation, and a chronic urban housing shortage.
The central concept is canonical rigidity: the tendency of territorial parish boundaries to persist long after the demographic conditions that justified them have changed. The two analyses here quantify the degree of that mismatch and explore its implications for service delivery efficiency and urban land use.


Spatial Analysis →
The main analysis. Theoretical framework (Hotelling, Huff gravity model), identification strategy (Voronoi counterfactuals, Canonical Leakage Index), and econometric analysis of the service-density elasticity. Includes case studies of three cross-boundary metro areas — Cincinnati/Covington, New York/Brooklyn, and Chicago/Joliet — where physical geography produces the clearest examples of canonical leakage.


Redevelopment Analysis →
A ranked set of candidate sites where service underutilization, population density, and surface parking footprint (Overture Maps verified) jointly indicate a severe mismatch between institutional use and urban land economics. Searchable table and interactive map covering all major US dioceses.

Built in R (sf, tidyverse) and Python (Overture Maps API), rendered with Quarto.

title: Redevelopment Analysis: Priority Sites by Diocese
text:
The main analysis identifies the structural conditions under which canonical rigidity generates asset misallocation: parishes in high-density urban areas holding large surface parking footprints while offering fewer services than their surrounding population would predict. This page translates that framework into a ranked set of candidate sites.
The Redevelopment Index is a composite score across three dimensions:
\[\text{Redev Score}_i = f\!\left(\text{PopDensity}_i,\; \text{ParkingArea}_i,\; \frac{1}{\text{MassFrequency}_i}\right)\]
Higher scores indicate greater misalignment between current institutional use and the potential value of the underlying land. Parishes are filtered to urban and suburban density tiers (>500 persons/km²) to focus on areas where the opportunity cost of surface parking is meaningful.

title: Redevelopment Analysis: Priority Sites by Diocese
text:
On the Policy Logic
The redevelopment argument is not that churches should close — it is that the specific sites flagged here represent a category where the mismatch between institutional use and urban land economics is particularly acute. A parish offering 6 weekend Masses in a neighborhood with 4,000 residents per km² and 5,000 m² of surface parking is, from a land-use standpoint, an outlier. What exactly should happen to that site involves canonical, historic preservation, and community considerations well outside the scope of this analysis.
The more tractable proposal is the ground-lease model: dioceses retain ownership of sacred structures while leasing surface parking to developers for multi-family residential construction. This preserves the parish’s sacramental function, removes no seats from the nave, and converts dead land into a stable endowment-style revenue stream — a structure that Catholic Charities Housing and similar organizations have piloted in several dioceses.

Infrastructure footprints from Overture Maps Foundation (May 2026 release). Revenue and population data from ACS 2022 5-Year Estimates.
